frase_gancho.texto: A Christ of the Ascension instead of the crucified Christ, a door that grants forgiveness, and a Gothic vault beneath the choir.

puente_narrativo.texto: Raise your eyes to the walls of the nave: there are the murals of the martyrs of Japan.

guion_corto.texto: Why is the Christ of this cathedral not crucified? Because here Jesus is shown at the Ascension, rising to heaven. That is how a guide to the cathedral describes it. The nave is wide and austere, like that of a sixteenth-century Franciscan convent. Beneath the choir lies the sotocoro, the space covered by the gallery above. According to México Desconocido, it has Gothic tracery and one of the oldest depictions of the Virgin of Guadalupe, a claim worth confirming. On the north façade is the Porciúncula Door. Franciscan tradition says that whoever passes through that door under the conditions set by the Church obtains the plenary indulgence known as the Pardon of Assisi.

guion_largo.texto:
Most Catholic churches have a crucified Christ above the altar. This one does not. A guide to the church says that the main image represents Jesus at the Ascension, rising to heaven.

The church has the plan of a Latin cross, with a single nave, and it is oriented from east to west. Many Franciscan churches of the period were like this: simple, with a single nave, designed for preaching. The interior has the austerity of a convent.

In the nineteenth century, the nave was filled with neoclassical altarpieces that covered the walls. Later, in the renovation of the 1950s, the main altar and the side altars were removed. That clearing revealed something that had been hidden for centuries: the murals of the martyrs of Japan. We will talk about them at the next two stops.

Later the main altarpiece was rescued and restored, in nineteen ninety-three. Earlier, in nineteen ninety-two, several paintings in the cathedral were protected thanks to the Adopt a Work of Art program.

From the center of the nave you can understand why the mural is so long. It covers the walls from the sotocoro to the chancel arch, which is the great arch that separates the nave from the presbytery. It is about thirty meters of painting that accompany anyone walking toward the altar.

The church has also suffered earthquakes. After the earthquake of two thousand seventeen, cracks appeared in the painted walls, and the plaster was protected. It is part of the life of a building that has stood for almost five centuries.

Beneath the choir is the sotocoro. The word is literal: the part that lies under the choir. According to one of the sources, it has Gothic tracery, that is, stone ribs that form patterns on the ceiling. Raise your eyes and follow those lines calmly. The ribs do not only hold up the ceiling: they also guide the gaze, which rises and then descends again toward the altar.

On the north wall is the Porciúncula Door. The name comes from the small chapel of the Porciúncula, near Assisi, in Italy, where Saint Francis asked for a special pardon for those who repented. Tradition calls it the Pardon of Assisi. Whoever passes through a door like this one, on the days and under the conditions that the Church establishes, may obtain a plenary indulgence. The conditions and the dates are defined by the Church.

Before going on, raise your eyes and lower your voice. If Mass is being held, wait a moment outside or walk through the church with respect. If you saw the atrium first, notice the change of light as you enter: from the open plaza you step into a more shaded nave. Speaking softly helps you hear the echo of the place. It is an active place of worship, not just a museum hall.

Stay a moment in the center of the nave. It is the best place to feel the scale of the church and to look at the long walls that, as you will see shortly, kept a thirty-meter painting.

texto: Find the main image of the church and notice whether the Christ is rising to heaven or crucified
Look beneath the choir and try to see the stone patterns on the ceiling
Find the north door, the Porciúncula Door, and ask what is requested when passing through it

texto.Plan: Latin cross, a single nave, east-west orientation
texto.North door: Porciúncula, linked to the Pardon of Assisi
texto.Sotocoro: with Gothic tracery, according to México Desconocido

texto.pregunta: Myth: All churches have a crucified Christ above the altar.
texto.respuesta: Reality: In this one, Jesus is represented at the Ascension, according to a guide to the church.
